items.title: The Price of a Cheap Jacket
items.text: Sora needed a winter jacket and found two choices. The first cost twenty dollars and looked fine in the shop. The second cost eighty dollars, which seemed far too much for a student, so she bought the cheap one. By the next winter its zipper had broken and the lining had torn, so she bought another. Over five winters she bought five cheap jackets, spent a hundred dollars, and was never really warm. Her cousin had paid for the better coat in the first year and was still wearing it, having spent nothing more. Sora realized that a low price tag shows only what you pay today, not what you will pay over time. A product that costs more at the start can be the cheaper choice in the end.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: A (A) price can hide a higher total cost, while a (B) item may save money over time.
o: high / fashionable
low / well-made
fair / discounted
low / second-hand
qs.why: 저렴한 가격은 총비용을 숨길 수 있고, 튼튼하게 만든 물건이 장기적으로 돈을 아낀다는 내용이에요.

qs.q: What is the main point of the passage?
o: The first price of a product is not always its true cost.
Students should never spend more than twenty dollars on clothes.
Winter jackets are made worse today than they were in the past.
Shop workers often hide the real prices of their goods.
qs.why: 초기 가격만으로는 실제 비용을 알 수 없다는 것이 요지예요.

qs.q: Which sentence best describes how Sora's view changed?
o: She decided never to spend money on winter clothes again.
She began to dislike the choices her cousin had made.
She came to believe that shops ought to lower their prices.
She stopped judging goods by their price alone.
qs.why: Sora는 가격표만 보고 판단하던 태도를 바꾸었어요.

qs.q: By the end of the story, how did Sora's spending compare with her cousin's?
o: She spent less but felt just as warm.
She spent the same but chose a better color.
She spent more and was less warm.
She spent less because her jackets were on sale.
qs.why: 다섯 벌에 100달러를 쓴 Sora는 80달러짜리 한 벌을 산 사촌보다 더 썼고 덜 따뜻했어요.

items.title: Trees on the Hottest Streets
items.text: On a summer afternoon, a paved street can be ten degrees hotter than a nearby park. Concrete and dark roads soak up sunlight all day and release it slowly after sunset, so neighborhoods with few trees stay warm even at night. Trees work in the opposite way. Their leaves block direct sunlight, and the water that evaporates from them cools the surrounding air. Several cities have therefore begun planting trees along the hottest streets first, rather than spreading them evenly. Early results are encouraging: residents say that walking outdoors feels easier, and some buildings use less electricity for air conditioning. Planting takes years to show its full effect, however, because young trees give little shade. Planners say the goal is not decoration but protecting people, especially older adults, from dangerous heat.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Hard surfaces (A) heat in cities, whereas trees (B) the air, so planting them on the hottest streets can protect residents.
o: repel / cool
store / cool
store / warm
create / dry
qs.why: 도로는 열을 흡수해 저장했다가 내보내고, 나무는 공기를 식혀 줘요.

qs.q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How planting trees can lower heat in the hottest parts of a city
Why city streets are repaired more often in summer than in winter
Why electricity bills are higher in cities than in the countryside
How planners choose which kinds of trees each neighborhood prefers
qs.why: 도시의 가장 더운 구역에 나무를 심어 열을 줄이는 방법이 중심 내용이에요.

qs.q: The word 'evenly' in the passage is closest in meaning to
o: in a short period of time
with great care near buildings
slowly over many years
in equal amounts everywhere
qs.why: 'spreading them evenly'는 어디에나 똑같이 퍼뜨린다는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: What can be inferred about the newly planted trees?
o: They will be removed when the summer is over.
They already give as much shade as old trees do.
Their cooling effect will increase as they grow.
They are planted mainly to make the streets look nicer.
qs.why: 어린 나무는 그늘이 적고 효과가 나타나려면 수년이 걸리므로 자라면서 효과가 커질 거라고 추론할 수 있어요.

items.title: Sleep and Memory
items.text: Many students believe that staying up all night before an exam is the best way to learn more. Sleep researchers disagree. During deep sleep, the brain replays what a person studied during the day and moves important information into long-term memory. When people skip sleep, this process is cut short, and they remember less the next morning, even if they studied for hours. In one classroom experiment, two groups learned the same list of words. The group that slept normally recalled far more words the next day than the group that stayed awake. The researchers do not suggest that studying is unnecessary; effort still matters. Their point is that rest is part of learning, not a waste of study time. A short night may feel like extra time, but it quietly removes what was gained.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Students who give up (A) to study longer may remember less, because the brain uses sleep to (B) new information.
o: sleep / delete
sleep / store
friends / store
exercise / lose
qs.why: 수면을 포기하면 뇌가 정보를 장기 기억으로 저장하는 과정이 줄어들어요.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the writer's main point?
o: Rest supports learning instead of wasting study time.
Studying for many hours is useless for exam preparation.
Researchers prefer group experiments to individual study.
Students should sleep less in order to remember more words.
qs.why: 휴식은 학습의 일부라는 것이 글의 요지예요.

qs.q: Why does the writer mention the experiment with two groups?
o: To prove that studying hard is unnecessary for exams
To compare two schools that have different sleep rules
To show that word lists are the best way to study
To give evidence for the claim about sleep and recall
qs.why: 실험은 잠이 기억에 도움이 된다는 주장을 뒷받침하는 증거예요.

qs.q: According to the passage, what does the brain do during deep sleep?
o: It rests completely and stops handling new information.
It deletes older facts so that new words can fit in.
It replays what was learned and stores it.
It prepares the body to study for longer hours.
qs.why: 깊은 잠 동안 뇌는 공부한 내용을 되풀이해 장기 기억으로 옮겨요.

items.title: Attention in a Noisy Feed
items.text: Social media is often blamed for shortening our attention, but the truth is more complicated. Apps are designed to offer a steady stream of small rewards, such as a new photo or a friendly comment, and the brain learns to check for them again and again. Over time, people may find it harder to stay with a long book or a single task. Yet researchers warn against simple conclusions. Some users learn quickly from short videos, and online groups help shy people find friends who share their interests. The difference seems to lie in how the apps are used rather than whether they are used. People who set limits and choose carefully tend to feel in control, while those who scroll without a purpose report feeling tired and distracted.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: The effect of social media on attention depends less on (A) than on (B) it is used.
o: how long it lasts / why
whether it is used / how
who designs the app / when
what it costs / where
qs.why: 핵심은 사용 여부가 아니라 사용 방식이에요.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
o: Social Media and Attention: It Depends on Use
Why Every Teenager Should Delete Social Apps
The Secret Rewards Hidden in Online Photos
How Short Videos Replaced Long Books for Good
qs.why: 사용 방식에 따라 영향이 달라진다는 균형 잡힌 내용이에요.

qs.q: What does the writer imply by saying 'researchers warn against simple conclusions'?
o: Researchers have not studied social media for a very long time.
Most people already know exactly how apps change the brain and mind.
Social media apps should be banned for everyone until more is known.
The effects of social media cannot be described as only good or bad.
qs.why: 단순한 결론을 경계한다는 것은 좋다/나쁘다로만 말할 수 없다는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: Which people report feeling tired and distracted?
o: Those who choose carefully and set limits
Those who join online groups about hobbies
Those who scroll without a clear purpose
Those who only watch short educational videos
qs.why: 목적 없이 스크롤하는 사람들이 피곤하고 산만하다고 해요.

items.title: The Museum Without Walls
items.text: Many museums now put their collections online, and some visitors wonder whether anyone will bother to enter the building again. Curators are not worried. A screen can show a painting in bright detail, let you zoom in on a tiny crack, and reach someone who lives thousands of kilometers away. What it cannot do is show the real size of an object, the texture of old paint, or the feeling of standing quietly in a room full of history. Surveys suggest that people who explore a collection online are actually more likely to visit later, because the website makes them curious. In this way, the two experiences support each other. The online version opens the door, and the visit completes the story.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Online collections (A) real visits instead of replacing them, because a website can make people (B) enough to come in person.
o: discourage / unhappy
encourage / curious
replace / careful
encourage / tired
qs.why: 온라인 전시는 호기심을 일으켜 실제 방문을 늘려 줘요.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Online and real museum visits work together rather than compete.
Museums will soon close their buildings and move everything online for good.
Paintings always look better on a screen than they do on a gallery wall.
Curators plan to charge visitors for viewing the website.
qs.why: 온라인과 실제 관람은 서로를 보완한다는 것이 요지예요.

qs.q: Which of the following can a screen NOT offer, according to the passage?
o: A bright picture of a painting in detail
The chance to zoom in on a tiny crack
Access for people who live thousands of kilometers from the museum
The feeling of standing in a room full of history
qs.why: 화면이 줄 수 없는 것은 실제 공간에서 느끼는 분위기예요.

qs.q: The sentence 'The online version opens the door' means that the website
o: shows how to build a new museum entrance
lets visitors enter the building without tickets
leads people toward visiting the museum
makes the real museum less interesting
qs.why: 문을 연다는 비유는 방문의 계기가 된다는 뜻이에요.

items.title: Learning a Language Abroad
items.text: Moving to another country is often described as the fastest way to learn a language, and in many ways it is. Learners hear the language all day, need it to buy food or ask for directions, and get quick feedback when they make mistakes. However, immersion does not guarantee progress. Some people spend most of their time with others from their own country and use the new language only a few minutes a day. Others learn very slowly because they are afraid of sounding foolish. By contrast, students in a well-planned classroom at home can study grammar step by step and practice speaking with a patient teacher. The best results seem to come from combining both: real conversations to build confidence, and careful study to fix patterns that mistakes make permanent.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Living abroad gives learners plenty of (A), but progress still depends on how much they actually (B) the language.
o: grammar / avoid
exposure / use
teachers / hear
money / study
qs.why: 해외 생활은 노출을 주지만 실제로 언어를 사용하는 양이 중요해요.

qs.q: Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Immersion helps, but it works best when combined with careful study.
Classrooms at home are always better than living abroad.
Learners should avoid people from their own country completely.
Making mistakes is the main reason people stop learning.
qs.why: 몰입 학습과 체계적 학습을 결합하는 것이 가장 좋다는 내용이에요.

qs.q: What is the writer's purpose in the sentence beginning 'By contrast'?
o: To prove that living abroad is a waste of time and money
To describe the writer's own experience in a language classroom
To warn students about expensive language schools in other countries
To introduce an alternative way of learning with its own strengths
qs.why: By contrast는 대안적 학습 방식의 장점을 소개해요.

qs.q: Which of the following is mentioned as a problem of living abroad?
o: Having almost no chance to hear the language spoken during the day
Not being able to find a patient teacher in the city
Spending most of the time with people from one's own country
Learning grammar in a step-by-step order
qs.why: 같은 나라 사람들과만 시간을 보내면 새 언어를 거의 쓰지 않아요.

items.title: Why Bees Matter
items.text: Bees are best known for honey, but their larger job is pollination. When a bee moves from flower to flower, it carries pollen that allows plants to produce fruit and seeds. A large share of the crops people eat, including apples, almonds and many vegetables, depends at least partly on this work. In recent years, beekeepers in several regions have reported that more colonies than usual are dying each winter. Scientists point to a mix of causes, such as disease, certain farm chemicals and the loss of wild flowers. No single cause explains everything, which makes the problem harder to solve. Farmers who leave strips of wild flowers beside their fields have seen healthier bees nearby. Such small changes suggest that protecting bees is possible if many people take part.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Bees are (A) for food crops, yet their numbers are falling for (B) reasons, so protecting them requires many people to act.
o: harmful / one
essential / several
optional / several
essential / unknown
qs.why: 벌은 작물에 필수적이고 감소 원인은 여러 가지예요.

qs.q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: The importance of bees and the difficulty of protecting them
The best way for beekeepers to produce honey on a small family farm
The differences between wild and farm animals
Why almonds are more popular than apples
qs.why: 벌의 중요성과 보호의 어려움이 중심 내용이에요.

qs.q: What does 'No single cause explains everything' suggest?
o: Scientists have found out nothing at all about the problem so far.
Disease is the least important of the causes.
Beekeepers are responsible for most of the damage.
Solving the problem will require several kinds of action.
qs.why: 원인이 여러 가지이므로 해결책도 여러 가지여야 한다는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: Why does the writer mention farmers who leave strips of wild flowers?
o: To criticize farmers for wasting their land on flowers
To explain how honey is made in the fields
To show that a small, practical step can help
To prove that chemicals are the only danger
qs.why: 야생화 띠 사례는 작은 실천도 도움이 된다는 걸 보여 줘요.

items.title: Working From Home, Working Apart
items.text: After years of remote work, many companies are asking employees to return to the office for part of the week. Supporters of working from home point out that it saves commuting time, lets people arrange their day around family needs, and often produces quiet, focused hours. Critics worry about something less visible: the small, unplanned conversations that happen by the coffee machine. These chats spread ideas, help new workers learn unwritten rules, and build trust that is hard to create through scheduled video calls. Neither side is entirely right. Surveys show that people who spend two or three days in the office report both higher satisfaction and stronger teamwork than those who are always at home or always at work. A flexible mixture, many managers conclude, offers more than either extreme.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Remote work offers (A), while office work offers (B), so a mixture of the two may be the most satisfying choice.
o: casual contact / focus and flexibility
focus and flexibility / casual contact
long commutes / quiet hours
video calls / long commutes
qs.why: 재택은 집중과 유연성을, 사무실은 비공식 교류를 줘요.

qs.q: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
o: A balance of home and office work can give the benefits of both.
Employees should be forced to work in the office every day.
Video calls build stronger trust than face-to-face talks.
Commuting is the main reason people dislike their jobs.
qs.why: 재택과 출근을 섞는 것이 둘의 장점을 모두 준다는 요지예요.

qs.q: What does the writer mean by 'something less visible'?
o: A problem that only the managers of large offices can notice
A rule that is written on the office wall
A kind of technology hidden inside computers
A benefit that is hard to see but still important
qs.why: 눈에 잘 띄지 않지만 중요한 사무실의 비공식 대화를 가리켜요.

qs.q: According to the surveys, who report higher satisfaction?
o: People who work from home on most days of the week
People who work in the office five days every week
People who work in the office two or three days a week
People who change jobs every year or every two years
qs.why: 주 2~3일 출근하는 사람들의 만족도가 가장 높았어요.

items.title: Lost Libraries, New Libraries
items.text: A century ago, a public library was a quiet place with shelves, a few tables and a strict librarian. Today, many libraries still lend books, but visitors may also borrow tools, join coding classes, record music in a small studio or get help with job applications. Some critics argue that libraries have lost their purpose now that so much information is free online. Librarians reply that free information is not the same as useful information. Many people lack a fast connection, a quiet room or the skills to judge which websites can be trusted. By offering these things, libraries serve the same old goal, helping people learn, in a form that fits the present. The building changes; the mission does not.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Modern libraries have changed what they (A), but their basic (B) of supporting learning remains the same.
o: forbid / budget
offer / mission
sell / silence
offer / location
qs.why: 도서관은 제공하는 서비스는 바뀌었지만 학습을 돕는 사명은 그대로예요.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Libraries have adapted to new needs while keeping their purpose.
Libraries are no longer needed because information is free.
Librarians dislike the new activities in their buildings.
Coding classes are more important than books and other printed material.
qs.why: 도서관이 목적은 유지한 채 변화에 적응했다는 요지예요.

qs.q: What does 'The building changes; the mission does not' mean?
o: Libraries move into new buildings every few years.
Librarians have given up their old jobs completely.
The mission of a library is still to keep all of its readers quiet and calm.
The services differ, but the goal of helping people learn is constant.
qs.why: 건물(서비스)은 바뀌어도 목적은 변하지 않는다는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: Why do librarians say 'free information is not the same as useful information'?
o: Online information is always wrong and misleading for most ordinary users.
Libraries charge less than websites for the same facts.
Many people cannot easily use or judge what they find online.
People prefer to read slowly rather than search quickly.
qs.why: 연결, 공간, 판단 능력이 부족한 사람이 많다는 뜻이에요.

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Leftovers
items.text: When we think about food waste, we imagine spoiled vegetables at the back of a refrigerator. But food is also lost earlier, in fields where oddly shaped fruit is thrown away, in warehouses with poor storage, and in shops that discard goods before the date printed on the label. At home, people buy more than they need because large packages look like a bargain. When the extra food is wasted, the money, water and energy used to grow it are wasted too. Some families have reduced their waste by planning meals for the week and freezing what they cannot eat in time. Others learn to read labels carefully, since a date stamped as 'best before' often refers to quality, not safety. Small habits, repeated daily, can make a surprising difference.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Food is wasted at (A) stages, from fields to kitchens, but simple (B) at home can reduce the loss.
o: few / prices
many / habits
late / recipes
many / stores
qs.why: 음식 낭비는 여러 단계에서 생기고 가정의 작은 습관이 줄여 줘요.

qs.q: Which is the best title for the passage?
o: Food Waste Begins Long Before the Refrigerator
How to Cook a Cheap Meal for Large Families
The Safest Dates for Eating Old Food
Why Odd-Shaped Fruit Tastes Better
qs.why: 음식 낭비는 냉장고 이전 단계에서도 일어난다는 내용이에요.

qs.q: Why do people buy more food than they need, according to the passage?
o: Shops give away extra food at the door.
They are afraid of running out of water.
They want to throw away food on purpose.
Large packages seem to be a good deal.
qs.why: 큰 포장이 더 싸 보여서 필요 이상으로 사요.

qs.q: What does the writer say about a 'best before' date?
o: It means the food must be thrown away that day.
It is printed only on frozen goods.
It often tells about quality rather than safety.
It is decided by each customer when the food is bought.
qs.why: 'best before'는 대개 안전이 아니라 품질을 가리켜요.

items.title: What Volunteers Really Receive
items.text: People usually describe volunteering as a gift: time given freely to help someone else. Yet many volunteers say they receive at least as much as they give. A teenager who tutors younger children may discover patience she did not know she had. A retired engineer who repairs bicycles for a community center finds a reason to leave the house each morning. Researchers who followed volunteers over several years found that they reported less loneliness and a stronger sense of purpose than similar people who did not volunteer. This does not mean that helping others should be done only for personal benefit. Rather, the finding suggests that giving and receiving are closely connected, and that a community grows stronger when everyone has a chance to do both.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Volunteering is not only a (A) to others but also a source of (B) for the volunteers themselves.
o: loan / debt
gift / benefit
gift / pressure
duty / boredom
qs.why: 봉사는 남에게 주는 선물이면서 봉사자에게도 이익이 돼요.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Helping others also brings real rewards to the helper.
Teenagers make better volunteers than retired people.
Volunteering should be done only when it benefits you.
Community centers need more engineers.
qs.why: 봉사는 하는 사람에게도 보상이 된다는 내용이에요.

qs.q: What did the researchers find?
o: Volunteers had more free time than other people.
Non-volunteers were happier in the long run.
Volunteers earned more money over several years.
Volunteers felt less lonely and more purposeful.
qs.why: 봉사자들은 외로움이 덜하고 목적의식이 컸어요.

qs.q: The writer includes the sentence 'This does not mean...' in order to
o: introduce a completely new topic
describe a volunteer's daily schedule
prevent a misunderstanding of the findings
criticize researchers who study volunteers
qs.why: 연구 결과를 오해하지 않도록 한계를 짚는 문장이에요.

items.title: Pen or Keyboard?
items.text: Taking notes by typing is faster, and the result is neat and easy to search. For these reasons, many students prefer laptops in lectures. Some studies, however, suggest that handwriting may lead to better understanding. Because people write more slowly than a teacher speaks, they cannot record every word. They have to listen, decide what matters, and put it into their own words. Typists often copy sentences nearly word for word without thinking about them. As a result, when tested on ideas rather than facts, students who wrote by hand sometimes perform better. The advantage is not guaranteed; a careful typist can also summarize well, and a distracted writer may learn very little. The key factor seems to be the thinking that happens while taking notes, not the tool itself.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Handwriting may help understanding because it forces students to (A) the content, but what finally matters is the (B) during note-taking.
o: copy / speed
select / thinking
ignore / thinking
select / neatness
qs.why: 손글씨는 내용을 선별하게 하지만 결국 중요한 것은 필기 중의 사고예요.

qs.q: Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: The thinking involved in note-taking matters more than the tool used.
Handwriting is always better than typing for every student.
Typing is faster and therefore the better method of learning.
Teachers should speak more slowly in every lecture.
qs.why: 도구보다 필기하며 하는 생각이 중요하다는 결론이에요.

qs.q: Why do typists often copy sentences nearly word for word?
o: They are not allowed to use their own words.
They prefer to avoid hearing the lecture.
They have trouble reading the screen.
They can type as fast as the teacher speaks.
qs.why: 타이핑은 말하는 속도만큼 빨라서 그대로 옮기기 쉬워요.

qs.q: The word 'advantage' in the passage is closest in meaning to
o: disadvantage
habit
benefit
price
qs.why: advantage는 '이점'이라는 뜻이고 benefit과 가장 가까워요.

items.title: Gardens Above the Street
items.text: Rooftop gardens are spreading across crowded cities, and their supporters promise fresh vegetables, cooler buildings and a closer link between people and food. The reality is mixed. A rooftop farm can supply a neighborhood restaurant or a school kitchen, but it cannot feed a whole city; the space is simply too small. Soil is heavy, so buildings must be strong enough to carry it, and watering needs careful planning. Even so, urban farms offer benefits that are hard to measure in kilograms. Children who plant seeds learn where food comes from, and neighbors who work together often become friends. Growers therefore describe their projects less as a replacement for traditional farming and more as a classroom, a meeting place and a small step toward a more connected city.

items.title: Setting the World's Clocks
items.text: Until about two hundred years ago, every town set its clocks by the sun, so noon in one place came minutes later than noon in a town to the east. This caused little trouble when travel was slow. Railways changed that. A traveler crossing a country might need to adjust a watch many times, and timetables became a confusing puzzle that sometimes caused accidents. The solution was to divide the world into zones, each with one standard time. Not everyone welcomed the change; some towns felt they were giving up their own local time for the convenience of distant companies. Today the system is so familiar that we rarely notice it, although scheduling an online meeting across several zones shows that time is still something we must organize together.

items.title: A City Beneath the Waves
items.text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter about a quarter of all sea species. The reason is that a reef is a living city. Tiny animals called corals build hard skeletons that form a structure where fish hide, feed and raise their young. Corals also depend on algae that live inside them and give them food and color. When the water becomes too warm, corals push the algae out and turn white, a condition known as bleaching. A bleached reef is not dead, but it is weak, and if the heat lasts too long, it can die. Scientists are testing ways to help reefs recover, such as growing heat-tolerant corals, but they stress that the most important step is to limit the warming of the sea.

items.title: The Value of Being Wrong
items.text: In many classrooms, a wrong answer is treated as an embarrassment. Students learn to avoid risks, and the quiet ones may never raise their hands. Yet people who study learning argue that mistakes are among the most useful signals a mind can receive. When we are wrong, we notice a gap between what we believed and what is true, and that gap is exactly where learning takes place. Teachers who encourage students to explain why an answer failed often see deeper understanding than teachers who only mark answers right or wrong. Of course, this does not mean that mistakes are pleasant, or that careless errors do not matter. It means that a mistake becomes valuable only when someone looks at it honestly. A classroom that allows this is not lowering its standards; it is raising the quality of its thinking.

items.title: The Third Kind of Traveler
items.text: Electric bicycles are now a common sight in many cities. Their motor makes hills and long distances easier, so people who would never cycle to work on an ordinary bike begin to do so. City officials welcome this change because every trip on an e-bike may replace a trip by car. But the new popularity brings problems. Some riders travel faster than pedestrians expect, and narrow paths shared by walkers and cyclists have become tense. Parking and charging are also unsolved questions. Experts propose wider lanes, lower speed limits in busy areas and clear rules about where batteries may be charged. Their message is that the bicycle is not the problem; the problem is that streets built for cars and walkers have not yet been redesigned for a third kind of traveler.

items.title: The Lantern Festival Grows Up
items.text: Every autumn, a small mountain village holds a lantern festival that once belonged only to its residents. Families made paper lanterns, walked together to the hill and shared rice cakes under the moon. In recent years, visitors from nearby cities have arrived by the thousand. The village has earned money, repaired its road and opened a small cafe. But some elders feel uneasy. The path is crowded, the lanterns are now mass-produced for sale, and many young residents spend the festival working at food stalls instead of walking with their families. A committee has begun to limit the number of visitors and has asked each family to make at least one lantern by hand. They hope the festival can welcome guests without losing the quiet meaning that made it worth visiting.

items.title: Music, Silence and Study
items.text: Some people say they cannot work without music; others need silence. Research suggests both groups may be right, depending on the task. Quiet music without words can raise mood and help people stay with simple, repetitive jobs. However, when the task is reading or writing something complicated, songs with lyrics compete with the words in the mind, and performance drops. The loudness of the surroundings matters too. A low background hum, like the sound of a cafe, seems to encourage creative thinking, while sudden loud sounds interrupt it. The practical advice is not to follow one rule but to match the sound to the work. If you notice your attention slipping, changing the sound or choosing silence for a while may be the easiest improvement you can make.

Summary: The best background sound depends on the (A) of the task: music can help with (B) jobs, but lyrics disturb reading.

items.title: Do Stories Make Us Kinder?
items.text: Does reading stories make people kinder? Some psychologists believe it can. When we read a novel, we follow a character's thoughts, fears and choices for hours, and this practice may help us imagine how others feel. In several studies, people who had just read a short story scored slightly higher on tests that ask them to read emotions in photographs of eyes. Not every researcher is convinced. They point out that people who already care about others may simply enjoy fiction more, so the connection might run in the opposite direction. The debate is unlikely to end soon. What both sides agree on is that stories offer a safe way to experience lives very different from our own, and that this experience, even if its long-term effect is small, is rarely harmful.

items.title: The Real Price of a Cheap Shirt
items.text: Fast fashion companies release new styles every few weeks and sell them at prices so low that clothes feel almost disposable. Shoppers enjoy the variety, and many cannot afford to spend more. The hidden price, however, is paid elsewhere: large amounts of water and chemicals go into dyeing cloth, and mountains of unwanted garments end up in landfills. Some companies now promise recycled fibers and repair services, but critics say these steps are small compared with the speed of production. Individuals can help by buying fewer items, choosing durable ones and passing clothes on to others. The most effective change, many experts add, is a shift in attitude, from asking 'Is this cheap?' to asking 'How long will I wear it?'

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

items.title: Rubbish Above the Sky
items.text: Since the first satellite was launched, thousands of objects have been placed in orbit. Many are now useless: old rockets, broken satellites and tiny pieces of metal and paint. Traveling at several kilometers per second, even a fleck of paint can damage a working spacecraft. The danger grows because collisions create more fragments, which in turn raise the chance of further collisions. Engineers track larger pieces and move satellites out of the way when necessary, yet they cannot track the smallest ones. Newer satellites are designed to leave orbit safely when their work is done, and some teams are testing methods to capture old objects. Experts agree that prevention is easier than cleanup: it is much simpler not to leave waste in space than to retrieve it afterwards.

items.title: More Than Talent
items.text: A team of talented athletes does not always beat a team of friends who understand each other. Coaches often say that individual skill wins moments but cooperation wins seasons. Cooperation in sport means more than passing the ball. Players must predict how teammates will move, accept different roles and sometimes give up a chance to score so that someone else can. Such choices are possible only when players trust one another. Trust grows through shared practice, honest talk after defeats and respect for the person who sits on the bench. Some research on workplace teams finds a similar pattern: groups that feel safe to admit mistakes tend to solve problems faster. The lesson reaches beyond the field: success is rarely a solo performance.

items.title: Lost in Translation
items.text: Machine translation has improved so much that travelers can point a phone at a menu and read it instantly. For simple, practical messages, the results are often good enough. Still, language is more than a list of words. Humor, politeness and cultural references rarely survive a word-for-word conversion. A phrase that sounds friendly in one language may seem rude in another. Professional translators therefore see software as a helpful assistant rather than a replacement. They use it for a first draft, then check tone and meaning with their own knowledge of both cultures. For learners, translation tools can be useful, but depending on them too heavily may prevent the slow practice that builds real fluency.

items.title: Every Drop Counts
items.text: In dry regions, farmers have long lost much of their water before it reaches the plants. When a field is flooded, a large share evaporates or sinks into the ground beyond the roots. Drip irrigation solves part of this problem by delivering small amounts of water directly to each plant through thin tubes. Farms that adopt it often use far less water and sometimes harvest more, since the soil stays evenly moist. The system is not perfect. It costs money to install, the tubes can become blocked, and poorer farmers may find the price too high. Some governments and local groups offer loans or shared equipment. Such support suggests that technology alone cannot change farming; it must be paired with ways of making it available to those who need it most.

items.title: A Later Bell
items.text: Several schools have experimented with starting the day an hour later for teenagers. The idea rests on biology: during adolescence the body clock shifts, so many teens naturally fall asleep late and struggle to wake early. In schools that changed their schedules, students reported sleeping longer, and teachers noticed fewer students falling asleep in class. Some results were less clear. Attendance improved in certain schools but barely changed in others, and test scores did not always rise. Opponents raise practical concerns too: later endings can disturb sports practice, bus routes and the working hours of parents. Supporters answer that such problems can be managed, while chronic tiredness is harder to repair. The debate shows how a choice that looks like a simple schedule change can affect a whole community's routine.

items.title: Passion or Paycheck?
items.text: Young people choosing a field of study are often given two opposite pieces of advice: follow your passion, or choose a practical job. Both pieces have weaknesses. Passion can fade when it meets the daily routine of real work, and many interests begin only after a person has become skilled. On the other hand, a career chosen only for salary can feel empty after a few years, and job markets change faster than predictions. Counselors increasingly suggest a middle path: begin with what you do reasonably well, notice what keeps your attention, and be ready to adjust. In this view, a career is not a single decision made at eighteen but a series of choices, each guided by what you have learned about yourself.

items.title: Owning Less
items.text: Minimalism is sometimes pictured as a white room with one chair, but many people who practice it describe something simpler: owning fewer things so that each one matters. They say that fewer possessions mean less cleaning, less worry and more time for activities they value. Researchers add that having many choices can be tiring, and reducing them can make daily decisions easier. Critics reply that minimalism can become another form of showing off, particularly when people buy expensive items to look simple. They also note that those with little money have no choice about owning less, and for them, simplicity is not an option but a difficulty. The most convincing versions of minimalism, perhaps, are those that treat it as a tool for attention rather than a style.

items.title: The Power of Expecting
items.text: A placebo is a pill with no active medicine, yet patients who take one often feel better. This is not simple imagination. Expecting relief can change how the brain handles pain and stress, and in some studies people have even reported fewer symptoms when they knew the pill was a placebo. Researchers use placebos to test new drugs: if a drug does not work better than a placebo, it cannot be called effective. The effect has limits, however. A placebo cannot shrink a tumor or cure an infection; it mainly alters how a person experiences symptoms. This is why doctors take care not to depend on it. They hope to understand it, so that the real power of expectation can support, but never replace, proper treatment.

items.title: Following the Voice
items.text: Few of us now get lost, because a voice from the phone tells us where to turn. Yet some researchers worry that this convenience has a cost. When people follow directions without studying the route, they form weaker mental maps of the places they travel through. Taxi drivers who rely on memory, by contrast, show more activity in brain areas linked to navigation. This does not mean that GPS should be thrown away. It is safer and quicker, especially in unfamiliar areas. The suggestion is rather to use it with awareness: look at the map before leaving, notice landmarks along the way and sometimes try a route from memory. Like any tool, it serves us best when we stay in charge.

items.title: Money From the Crowd
items.text: Crowdfunding lets inventors, artists and neighbors raise money from many small donors instead of one large investor. A designer in a small town can present a project on a website and receive support from strangers around the world. The method has opened doors for people who would never have been approved by a bank. It also tests interest: a project that fails to attract donors learns early that its idea may not be wanted. But the system has weaknesses. Campaigns with attractive videos can raise money for products that never get finished, and those who give are rarely protected as customers are. Donors are therefore advised to read plans carefully and to give only what they can afford to lose.

items.title: Town or City?
items.text: People who move from a big city to a small town often expect peace and find it. Housing costs less, neighbors greet one another, and the pace of life slows. But there are trade-offs. Fewer shops, limited public transport and fewer job choices can make daily life harder, especially for young people with ambitious plans. City life offers the opposite mixture: opportunity, culture and variety, together with noise, crowding and expense. Studies of life satisfaction do not find that one setting is happier than the other. What matters more is the match between a person's priorities and the place: someone who values quiet and community may flourish in a town, while someone who values variety may feel restless there.

items.title: Fixing Things Together
items.text: In a repair cafe, volunteers help visitors mend broken toasters, torn clothes and wobbly chairs for free. The idea began as a way to cut waste, and it does: each fixed object is one less item thrown away. But organizers say the most valuable products are less visible. Visitors learn how things work, which makes them less afraid of trying repairs at home. Retired workers share skills that might otherwise be forgotten. Strangers sit at the same table, drinking tea and discussing how to open a stubborn lid. Some manufacturers make this harder by gluing parts together or refusing to sell spare ones, and campaigners push for laws that guarantee a 'right to repair'. Until then, the cafes show that a throwaway habit can be changed by neighbors working together.

items.title: Praise That Helps
items.text: Parents and teachers often praise children by saying, 'You are so smart!' It feels kind, but psychologists have found a hidden problem. Children who are praised for ability may start to see intelligence as fixed, and they avoid hard tasks that might reveal a weakness. In contrast, children praised for effort, strategy or improvement tend to take on difficult problems and recover faster from failure. The difference may seem small, yet it influences how children explain success. 'I worked hard on this' gives a student something to repeat; 'I am smart' offers nothing to do next time. This does not mean that kind words should be avoided. It means that the most helpful praise points to what a child did, not what a child is.

items.title: Two Languages, One Mind
items.text: People who speak two languages often switch between them without noticing. Scientists once feared that learning two languages at once would confuse children, but modern studies suggest otherwise. Bilingual children may take slightly longer to learn certain words in each language, yet their total vocabulary is similar to or larger than that of single-language peers. Some research finds that bilinguals are better at ignoring distractions, perhaps because their brains constantly choose which language to use. Not all studies agree, and the advantages are small in everyday life. What is clear is that bilingualism does no harm, and it brings obvious benefits: communication with more people, access to more stories and a deeper understanding of how languages work.

items.title: The Island That Needs Its Visitors
items.text: The island's main income comes from tourists who arrive each summer to enjoy its beaches. Water is limited, rubbish collection struggles in the high season, and rents have risen so much that some local families cannot afford to live near the coast. A few residents suggest a daily limit on visitors and a small fee that would fund cleaning and water supply. Business owners worry that fewer visitors will mean fewer customers. The debate is not about whether tourism is good or bad. It is about finding a level at which visitors can come without making the island a worse place to live.

items.title: A Thirty Percent Chance
items.text: When a forecast says there is a thirty percent chance of rain, many people think the forecast is wrong if the day stays dry. In fact, the statement describes probability, not a promise. It means that in similar conditions in the past, rain fell on about three out of ten occasions. Forecasters rely on computer models that simulate the atmosphere, but small differences in starting data can lead to different results, especially several days ahead. A single prediction can therefore never be perfectly certain. Understanding this helps us use forecasts wisely: a high chance of rain suggests carrying an umbrella, while a low chance suggests that we can take the risk. A forecast is not a verdict; it is a guide for making decisions with incomplete information.

qs.why: 30% 확률은 비슷한 조건에서 과거 열 번 중 약 세 번 비가 왔다는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Forecasts should be read as probabilities, not guarantees.
Forecasters are often careless with the data they collect each day.
It rains on three days out of every ten.
Umbrellas are unnecessary on dry days.
qs.why: 예보는 보장이 아니라 확률이라는 점이 요지예요.

qs.q: Why can predictions several days ahead differ?
o: Computers stop working properly after about one day of use.
Clouds disappear from the sky at night.
Forecasters change the model on purpose to surprise the public.
Small differences in starting data can change the results.
qs.why: 초기 자료의 작은 차이가 결과를 바꿀 수 있기 때문이에요.

qs.q: What does 'A forecast is not a verdict' mean?
o: It is always decided by a judge in a court of law.
It cannot be useful to anyone.
It does not give a final and certain judgment.
It is decided after the weather happens.
qs.why: 예보는 확정된 판정이 아니라는 뜻이에요.

items.title: Choosing the Summary
items.text:
Mina: Jun, have you finished reading the article about tidal energy?
Jun: Yes. It says the ocean's tides could supply steady power, unlike wind, which depends on the weather.
Mina: Right, but I noticed it also mentions high building costs.
Jun: True. The machines must survive salt water and strong currents, so repairs are expensive.
Mina: So how should we summarize it in one sentence for our report?
Jun: Maybe like this: tidal energy is reliable, but it is costly to build and maintain.
Mina: I like that, though I would add that engineers expect prices to fall as designs improve.
Jun: Good point. That shows the writer is hopeful, not only critical.
Mina: Then let's keep the first part short and spend more words on the future.
Jun: Agreed. I'll write the draft tonight, and you can check the grammar tomorrow.

qs.q: What are Mina and Jun mainly doing?
o: Arguing about who read the article first and who understood it
Preparing a one-sentence summary of an article
Choosing a topic for a science fair
Comparing the weather in two seas
qs.why: 두 사람은 기사를 한 문장으로 요약할 준비를 하고 있어요.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Tidal energy is (A) but expensive, although its cost may (B) in the future.
o: reliable / fall
unreliable / fall
reliable / rise
weak / disappear
qs.why: 조력 에너지는 안정적이지만 비싸고, 비용은 앞으로 내려갈 것으로 기대돼요.

qs.q: Why does Mina want to add the last part about engineers?
o: It proves that wind power is cheaper.
It explains why salt water is dangerous.
It makes the report longer than other reports.
It shows that the writer is hopeful about the future.
qs.why: 미래에 대한 낙관적 태도를 보여 주기 위해서예요.

qs.q: What will Jun do next?
o: Check Mina's grammar tomorrow
Visit a tidal power station with Mina
Write a draft of the summary tonight
Ask the engineers about prices
qs.why: Jun이 오늘 밤 초안을 쓰기로 했어요.

items.title: Too Much Detail
items.text:
Teacher: Daniel, I read your summary of the chapter on coral reefs.
Daniel: Did I miss something?
Teacher: Not exactly. You included every example, so it is almost as long as the chapter itself.
Daniel: I thought more details would make it better.
Teacher: A summary should keep the main claim and drop most of the examples. Ask yourself what the writer wants the reader to remember.
Daniel: So I should keep the idea that warm water harms reefs, but not the list of fish?
Teacher: Exactly. Mention one example only if it is needed to explain the claim.
Daniel: And what about my own opinion that reefs are beautiful?
Teacher: Save that for your discussion. A summary reports the writer's ideas, not yours.
Daniel: I understand. I'll cut it to three sentences and send it again tonight.

qs.q: What was the main problem with Daniel's summary?
o: It had too few details about the many fish species in a reef.
It was nearly as long as the chapter, with too many examples.
It was written in a language other than English.
It did not mention the title of the chapter.
qs.why: 예시를 모두 넣어 원문만큼 길어진 것이 문제예요.

qs.q: According to the teacher, what should a summary keep?
o: The main claim of the writer
Every example from the chapter
The summarizer's own feelings
A list of all the species
qs.why: 요약은 필자의 핵심 주장을 유지해야 해요.

qs.q: Why does the teacher say 'Save that for your discussion'?
o: Reefs are not beautiful at all, so his opinion is wrong.
Daniel's discussion is already finished.
The opinion is wrong and must be corrected.
Personal opinions do not belong in a summary.
qs.why: 요약에는 필자의 생각을 담고 개인 의견은 넣지 않기 때문이에요.

qs.q: What will Daniel most likely do next?
o: Add many more examples to every paragraph
Write about the beauty of reefs
Shorten the summary and submit it again
Ask another student to rewrite it
qs.why: 세 문장으로 줄여 다시 제출하겠다고 했어요.

items.title: Saturday Plans
items.text:
Sora: Should we go hiking on Saturday, or visit the science museum?
Hana: I'd like to hike, but the forecast says it will rain after lunch.
Sora: Then the mountain could be slippery in the afternoon.
Hana: Exactly. The museum is open all day, though it will probably be crowded.
Sora: What if we do both? We could hike in the morning and go to the museum after lunch.
Hana: That sounds good. The trail is short, so we can finish by noon.
Sora: Should we take the bus or ask my brother for a ride?
Hana: The bus is cheaper, but it only comes once an hour.
Sora: Then let's ask my brother. He can drop us at the trail and pick us up at the museum.
Hana: Perfect. I'll bring sandwiches for a quick lunch in the car.

qs.q: What problem do the two friends solve?
o: How to choose between two different science museums in the city
How to enjoy both an outdoor activity and an indoor one
Where to buy sandwiches on Saturday
How to avoid asking Sora's brother for help
qs.why: 야외 활동과 실내 활동을 모두 즐길 계획을 세워요.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Because rain is expected (A), they will hike (B) and visit the museum afterwards.
o: after lunch / in the morning
in the morning / after lunch
all day / at night
after lunch / on Sunday
qs.why: 점심 후에 비가 올 예정이라 오전에 하이킹을 하고 오후에 박물관에 가요.

qs.q: Why do they decide not to take the bus?
o: It is more expensive than a car.
It does not go near the museum.
It is too crowded on Saturdays.
It runs only once an hour.
qs.why: 버스가 한 시간에 한 대뿐이라 포기해요.

qs.q: What can be inferred about Sora's brother?
o: He dislikes both hiking and museums, so he will wait at home.
He will join them for the entire day.
He will help them travel between the two places.
He lives near the mountain trail.
qs.why: 그가 등산로에 내려 주고 박물관에서 태워 주는 역할이에요.

items.title: The Recycling Campaign Meeting
items.text:
Leader: Thanks for coming, everyone. We need to decide how to promote our recycling campaign.
Eun: I suggest posters in the hallways. They are cheap, and everyone walks past them.
Minho: But students rarely read posters. A short video on the school website might reach more people.
Eun: That's a fair point, but only a few students visit the website.
Leader: What if we make a video and show it during homeroom?
Minho: That would work, and we could use the posters as a reminder afterward.
Eun: Our budget is small, though. Posters need paper and color printing.
Leader: We can print them in black and white on used paper. That fits the theme of the campaign.
Minho: I like that. I can film the video this week if someone writes the script.
Eun: I'll write it. Let's show the video on Monday.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the meeting?
o: To choose a way to promote the recycling campaign
To collect used paper from every classroom
To choose a new leader for the recycling club
To plan a school trip to a recycling center
qs.why: 회의의 목적은 재활용 캠페인을 홍보할 방법을 정하는 것이에요.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Since few students read posters or visit the website, the club will show a (A) in homeroom and print (B) posters on used paper.
o: video / black-and-white
poster / color
video / color
script / large and colorful
qs.why: 영상은 조회 시간에 보여 주고 포스터는 재활용지에 흑백으로 인쇄해요.

qs.q: Why does the leader suggest printing posters on used paper?
o: It makes the posters easier to read.
It is required by the school rules.
It helps the posters last much longer.
It matches the theme of the campaign.
qs.why: 재활용 캠페인의 주제와 어울리기 때문이에요.

qs.q: Who will write the script?
o: Minho
The leader
Eun
A teacher
qs.why: Eun이 대본을 쓰겠다고 했어요.

items.title: Do Dolphins Ever Sleep?
items.text:
Host: Dr. Lee, many people believe that dolphins never sleep. Is that true?
Dr. Lee: Not exactly. Dolphins do rest, but they do it in an unusual way.
Host: How is it different from our sleep?
Dr. Lee: A dolphin must come to the surface to breathe, so it cannot fall completely unconscious. Instead, it rests one half of its brain at a time.
Host: So the other half stays awake?
Dr. Lee: Yes. That half controls breathing and keeps an eye on the surroundings. After a few hours, the halves switch roles.
Host: That sounds very practical. Do other animals do this?
Dr. Lee: Some birds appear to rest half of their brains while flying long distances, but dolphins are the best-known example.
Host: So the idea that dolphins never sleep is a myth.
Dr. Lee: It is a simplification. They do sleep, just not in the way humans do.

qs.q: What is the main point of Dr. Lee's explanation?
o: Dolphins never need any rest at all.
Dolphins sleep with half the brain resting at a time.
Dolphins sleep as deeply as humans do.
Dolphins breathe underwater without coming up.
qs.why: 돌고래는 뇌의 절반씩 번갈아 쉬며 잔다는 것이 핵심이에요.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: A dolphin cannot sleep deeply because it must (A) to breathe and needs to stay (B) to its surroundings.
o: surface / alert
dive / asleep
surface / hungry
hide / alert
qs.why: 호흡하려면 수면으로 올라와야 하고 주변을 살피며 깨어 있어야 해요.

qs.q: Why does Dr. Lee call the common idea 'a simplification'?
o: It is completely true in every case.
It was invented by the host.
It describes animals that fly.
It is partly true but leaves out how dolphins really rest.
qs.why: 돌고래가 아예 자지 않는다는 말은 일부만 맞고 실제 방식을 생략했다는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: What does the mention of birds show?
o: Birds cannot fly for long distances.
Birds sleep far more deeply than dolphins do at night.
Some other animals may also rest half the brain.
Dolphins were once a kind of bird that lived near the sea.
qs.why: 일부 새도 비슷하게 쉬는 것으로 보인다는 예를 들었어요.

items.title: The Screen Time Deal
items.text:
Tom: Dad said I can only use my tablet for one hour a day, but that's not enough.
Yuna: Why do you need more? You only play games.
Tom: That's not true. I also watch videos about drawing, and I practice what I learn.
Yuna: Hmm, that's different. Did you tell Dad about the drawing?
Tom: I tried, but he thinks I'm making excuses.
Yuna: Maybe you should show him your drawings. Evidence is stronger than words.
Tom: Good idea. What if I propose a deal? One hour for games, and an extra half hour for learning.
Yuna: That might work, especially if you keep a record of what you do during the extra time.
Tom: I'll make a chart this weekend and talk to him on Sunday.
Yuna: Don't forget to stay calm. Dad listens better when you don't argue.

qs.q: What does Tom want?
o: To stop drawing and spend all his time on games
More time on the tablet for learning to draw
To buy a new tablet with his own savings
To play games for the whole day
qs.why: 그림을 배우기 위한 추가 태블릿 시간을 원해요.

qs.q:
Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B).

Summary: Tom will offer his father a (A) and back it up with a (B) of his activities.
o: deal / record
gift / secret
deal / complaint
rule / game
qs.why: 추가 학습 시간을 거래로 제안하고 활동 기록으로 뒷받침해요.

qs.q: Why does Yuna suggest showing Dad the drawings?
o: Dad enjoys looking at drawings on tablets.
Tom's drawings are better than her own drawings.
Dad has already promised to give more time.
Evidence is more convincing than words alone.
qs.why: 증거가 말보다 설득력이 있다고 했어요.

qs.q: What advice does Yuna give for the talk with Dad?
o: Talk to him as soon as possible tonight
Pretend to agree with him
Stay calm instead of arguing
Bring a friend to help argue
qs.why: 침착하게 말하라고 조언해요.

items.q:
Volcanic eruptions destroy farms and villages, yet the ash they leave behind enriches the soil with minerals. Centuries later, the slopes of many volcanoes are among the most fertile land, which is why people keep returning to live there despite the danger.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Volcanoes (A) in the short term but can (B) the land in the long term.
o: enrich / destroy
destroy / enrich
cool / enrich
destroy / dry
items.why: 화산은 단기적으로 파괴하지만 장기적으로 토양을 비옥하게 만들어요.

items.q:
Bamboo grows quickly and bends in storms without breaking, while a stiff oak resists the wind until it snaps. In the same way, people who adapt to change often survive hardships that defeat those who refuse to bend.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Flexibility often helps more than (A), since what can (B) is less likely to break.
o: resistance / bend
speed / grow
resistance / snap
height / bend
items.why: 버티기보다 휘어질 수 있는 것이 덜 부러진다는 비유예요.

items.q:
A city park is more than green space. It gives children room to play, lets older residents meet friends, and offers workers a place to rest. However, parks need constant care; without funding for cleaning and repairs, they soon become unsafe.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Parks bring (A) benefits to many groups but need regular (B) to stay safe.
o: social / advertising
financial / maintenance
private / decoration
social / maintenance
items.why: 공원은 여러 집단에 사회적 이익을 주지만 안전을 위해 꾸준한 관리가 필요해요.

items.q:
Electric cars produce no exhaust, which improves the air in busy streets. But making their batteries uses large amounts of energy and minerals, and if the electricity comes from coal, much of the benefit is lost. The environmental value of an electric car therefore depends on how its power is produced.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Electric cars are (A) on the street, but their overall benefit depends on the (B) of the electricity.
o: slower / source
cleaner / price
cleaner / source
cheaper / the color
items.why: 전기차는 거리에서는 깨끗하지만 전체 효과는 전력의 생산 방식에 달려 있어요.

items.q:
Online reviews help shoppers compare products quickly. Yet some reviews are written by sellers or paid writers, and angry customers are more likely to post than satisfied ones. Reading the overall pattern, not single comments, gives a more reliable picture.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Reviews are (A) but not always (B), so shoppers should look at the overall pattern.
o: helpful / long
helpful / honest
rare / honest
costly / up to date
items.why: 후기는 유용하지만 항상 정직한 것은 아니므로 전체 경향을 봐야 해요.

items.q:
In some countries, people greet each other by shaking hands; in others, they bow or touch cheeks. A gesture that shows respect in one culture may feel strange or rude in another. Travelers who learn local customs avoid misunderstandings and show interest in their hosts.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Greeting customs (A) between cultures, so learning them helps travelers avoid (B).
o: differ / misunderstandings
match / misunderstandings
differ / unnecessary expenses
vanish / delays
items.why: 인사 방식은 문화마다 다르므로 배우면 오해를 피할 수 있어요.

items.q:
People often delay a task not because they are lazy, but because it feels unpleasant or too large. Breaking it into small steps makes the first move easier, and finishing one step creates the momentum to continue.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
People delay tasks that feel (A), and dividing a task into steps makes it (B) to begin.
o: enjoyable / easier
unpleasant / harder
short / harder
unpleasant / easier
items.why: 불쾌하게 느껴지는 일을 미루며, 단계로 나누면 시작하기 쉬워져요.

items.q:
Solar panels produce power only while the sun shines, so many homes use batteries to store extra energy for the evening. As battery prices fall, solar power becomes practical for more households, even in places with cloudy weather.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Batteries make solar energy (A) after dark, and falling prices make it (B) to more households.
o: wasted / attractive
usable / unavailable
usable / attractive
cheaper / hidden
items.why: 배터리가 밤에도 태양광을 쓸 수 있게 하고 가격 하락이 더 많은 가정에 매력적으로 만들어요.

items.q:
Children who are read to every day usually learn new words earlier. Listening to stories also teaches them how sentences are built and how stories are structured. The routine creates a warm bond between child and parent, which makes books feel enjoyable instead of like homework.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Daily story time builds (A) and makes reading feel (B).
o: vocabulary / difficult
vocabulary / enjoyable
speed / enjoyable
silence / required
items.why: 매일의 책 읽어 주기는 어휘를 늘리고 독서를 즐겁게 느끼게 해요.

items.q:
After a city charged a small fee for plastic bags, their use dropped sharply within months. Researchers said the amount of money mattered less than the extra moment of thought it forced: shoppers began to ask whether they really needed a bag.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
A small fee changed behavior because it made shoppers (A) before taking a bag, not because of the (B).
o: think / amount
hurry / amount
think / quality
complain / color
items.why: 소액 요금은 금액보다 한 번 더 생각하게 만들어서 효과가 있었어요.

items.q:
Experienced climbers often turn back before reaching the top if the weather worsens. They know that the summit is only halfway: the descent is where many accidents happen. For them, success means returning safely, not merely arriving.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Wise climbers value (A) over reaching the top, because (B) can be dangerous too.
o: speed / descending
safety / sleeping overnight
fame / climbing
safety / descending
items.why: 숙련된 등반가는 정상보다 안전을 중시하고 하산도 위험하다고 알아요.

items.q:
Languages never stand still. Words gain new meanings, such as 'mouse' for a computer device, and old words fall out of use. Some people see this as a decline, but linguists describe it as a sign of a living language that adapts to the needs of its speakers.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Changes in vocabulary show that a language is (A) rather than (B).
o: declining / alive
stable / adapting
alive / declining
alive / simple
items.why: 어휘의 변화는 언어가 쇠퇴하는 것이 아니라 살아 있다는 신호예요.

items.q:
Stores give loyalty cards because they want to learn what customers buy, not only to reward them. Each purchase adds to a record of habits, which helps the company decide what to stock and which discounts to offer. Customers get small savings; the store gets valuable information.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Loyalty cards give customers (A) and give stores (B).
o: information / small savings
small savings / information
free gifts / information
small savings / complaints
items.why: 고객은 소액 할인을, 가게는 구매 정보를 얻어요.

items.q:
The moon does not make its own light. We see it because it reflects sunlight, and its changing shape depends on how much of the sunlit half faces Earth. The moon itself never changes shape; only our view of it changes.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
The moon's phases come from our changing (A), not from any change in its (B).
o: view / shape
shape / view
distance / color
light / weight
items.why: 달의 위상은 우리 시점의 변화 때문이지 달 자체의 모양이 변해서가 아니에요.

items.q:
Before schools became common, many young people learned a trade by working beside a skilled adult. They watched, tried small tasks and slowly took on harder ones. Some educators argue that this gradual, hands-on approach still has value in classrooms.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Apprentices learned by (A) skilled adults, a (B) method some educators still admire.
o: obeying / theoretical
observing / written
paying / theoretical
observing / hands-on
items.why: 도제는 숙련자를 관찰하며 직접 해 보며 배웠고 일부 교육자는 이를 여전히 높이 평가해요.

items.q:
Many birds fly thousands of kilometers each year between summer and winter homes. They navigate using the sun, the stars and the earth's magnetic field. Scientists still do not fully understand how young birds that have never made the journey find their way.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Birds use several (A) to migrate, but scientists cannot yet fully explain how (B) birds find the way.
o: foods / young
signals / sleeping
signals / young
tools / old
items.why: 철새는 여러 단서로 길을 찾지만 어린 새가 어떻게 길을 찾는지는 완전히 설명되지 않았어요.

items.q:
Many prices end in 99 because the first digit looks smaller: a shopper sees 'nine' rather than 'ten'. Experiments show that people judge such a price as noticeably lower than it really is. The trick works even when buyers know about it, which shows how automatic first impressions can be.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Prices ending in 99 influence buyers through the (A) digit, and the effect works even when people are (B) of it.
o: last / aware
first / aware
first / unaware
middle / proud
items.why: 99로 끝나는 가격은 첫 숫자 때문에 효과가 있고, 구매자가 알고 있어도 작동해요.

items.q:
Giving children a small weekly allowance teaches money management better than lectures do. They discover that spending everything on the first day leaves nothing for later, and they learn to compare prices. Mistakes made with small sums are cheap lessons that prepare them for larger choices.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
An allowance teaches children to (A) money through (B) with small amounts.
o: manage / practice
earn / lectures
manage / lectures
waste / practice
items.why: 용돈은 적은 금액으로 직접 연습하며 돈 관리를 배우게 해요.

items.q:
Seed banks store samples of thousands of plant varieties at low temperatures. If disease or disaster destroys a crop, scientists can use the saved seeds to grow it again. These collections work like insurance: they cost little to keep and may prove priceless one day.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Seed banks work like (A), protecting future food supplies at a (B) cost.
o: insurance / high
markets / low
factories / small
insurance / low
items.why: 종자 은행은 적은 비용으로 미래의 식량을 지키는 보험과 같아요.

items.q:
Background music in shops is chosen carefully. Slow music makes shoppers walk slowly and spend more time looking, while fast music moves them along quickly in busy cafes. Customers rarely notice it, which is exactly why it is effective.

Choose the pair that best fills in (A) and (B) in the summary.
Shops use (A) music to guide customers' (B) without being noticed.
o: loud / hearing
background / opinions
background / behavior

items.q:
Some schools now let students choose their own seats at lunch rather than assigning tables by class. At first, teachers worried that groups would exclude others. In practice, students often sat with new classmates from shared clubs, and the lunchroom grew noisier but friendlier.

Which sentence is the best summary of the paragraph?
o: Assigned tables remain the surest way to keep a lunchroom quiet.
Free seating at lunch can lead students to make new friendships.
Teachers have banned school clubs because of conflicts at lunch.
Students who choose their seats prefer to eat alone each day.
items.why: 자유 좌석이 새로운 친구 관계로 이어졌다는 것이 요지예요.

items.q:
Cooking at home usually costs less than buying prepared meals, but the savings depend on planning. People who buy ingredients without a plan often throw away unused food, and the extra waste cancels out much of the difference. A weekly menu and a shopping list keep the benefit.

Which sentence is the best summary of the paragraph?
o: Home cooking saves money when meals are planned ahead.
Prepared meals are always cheaper than food cooked at home.
A weekly menu is more important than eating healthy food.
Throwing away unused ingredients is a good way to save money.
items.why: 계획 없이는 집밥의 절약 효과가 줄어든다는 내용이에요.

items.q:
When some museums began offering one free day a month, many expected crowds of the same regular visitors. Instead, surveys showed that a large share of free-day visitors had never been to a museum before. Free entry, it seems, can remove a barrier that curiosity alone cannot.

Which sentence is the best summary of the paragraph?
o: Regular visitors prefer museums that charge higher ticket prices.
Surveys prove that curiosity is more important than money.
Museums should be open only on one day of every month.
Free admission days can bring in people who rarely visit museums.
items.why: 무료 입장일이 박물관에 잘 가지 않던 사람들을 불러들였어요.

items.q:
Buildings in earthquake regions are no longer designed only to be rigid. Engineers now add flexible joints and heavy weights that move against the shaking, so that the structure absorbs energy instead of resisting it. Such buildings may sway, but they are far less likely to collapse.

Which sentence is the best summary of the paragraph?
o: Rigid buildings are safer than flexible ones in every earthquake.
Engineers add heavy weights mainly to make buildings look taller.
Modern buildings stay safe by absorbing shaking, not resisting it.
Swaying buildings are more likely to collapse than rigid ones.
items.why: 현대의 내진 설계는 흔들림을 흡수하는 방식이라는 점을 요약해야 해요.

items.q:
A community choir welcomes anyone who wants to sing, whether or not they can read music. Members say the weekly practice lowers stress, and singing in harmony gives a feeling of being part of something larger. Concerts are less important to them than the friendships formed at rehearsals.

Which sentence is the best summary of the paragraph?
o: Only skilled musicians should be allowed to join a community choir.
Joining a choir offers members relaxation and a sense of belonging.
Concerts are the main reason that people practice every week.
Reading music is the first thing a choir teaches its new members.
items.why: 합창단은 스트레스 해소와 소속감을 준다는 것이 요지예요.

items.q:
Many lighthouses once needed a keeper who lived on a lonely rock to light the lamp and warn passing ships. Automatic lights and satellite navigation have made this job unnecessary. Yet some towns preserve their lighthouses, because they have become symbols of the community's history rather than tools of safety.

Which sentence is the best summary of the paragraph?
o: Lighthouses lost their use but remain valued as history.
Satellite navigation has made every lighthouse more dangerous.
Lighthouse keepers still live on lonely rocks in most towns.
Towns destroy old lighthouses to build automatic lights instead.
items.why: 등대는 실용적 역할을 잃었지만 역사적 상징으로 보존된다는 내용이에요.

items.q:
A library once dropped its late-return fines. Librarians feared that books would never come back, but the opposite happened: more people returned overdue items, since they no longer felt embarrassed about owing money. The library also saw new visitors, including families who had stayed away because of earlier debts.

Which sentence is the best summary of the paragraph?
o: Fines are the only way to make readers return books.
Families avoid libraries because they enjoy owing money.
Librarians have discovered a cheaper way to buy new books.
Removing fines brought back both books and visitors.
items.why: 연체료를 없앴더니 책이 돌아오고 새 방문객이 늘었어요.

items.q:
Bicycle-sharing programs let people pick up a bike at one station and leave it at another. They work well for short trips across a city and reduce car traffic in the center. But bikes must be moved back to busy stations by trucks, which adds cost and pollution that planners often forget to count.

Which sentence is the best summary of the paragraph?
o: Trucks are the cheapest way to move people around a city.
Bicycle stations are always located in quiet neighborhoods.
Bike sharing eases traffic but has hidden costs.
Sharing programs have completely replaced cars in the center.
items.why: 자전거 공유는 교통을 줄이지만 재배치에 따른 숨은 비용이 있다는 내용이에요.

items.q:
Which word best completes the sentence?

____ the tickets were expensive, the concert was sold out within an hour.
o: Because of
Although
Unless
So that
items.why: 비싼 표에도 불구하고 매진되었다는 양보 관계이므로 Although가 알맞아요.

items.q:
The writer argues that cities should build more bike lanes. She explains that lanes reduce accidents and ease traffic. She also mentions that her own bicycle is blue and was a birthday present.

Which sentence would you leave out when summarizing the paragraph?
o: The writer's own bicycle is blue.
Bike lanes can reduce accidents.
Bike lanes can ease traffic.
Cities should build more bike lanes.
items.why: 자전거의 색깔은 요약에 필요하지 않은 세부 사항이에요.

items.q:
Which sentence has the same meaning as the one below?

Not only did the experiment fail, but it also wasted a month of work.
o: The experiment succeeded although it took a month.
The experiment failed because it lasted a month.
The experiment was cancelled after a month of success.
The experiment failed and also cost a month of work.
items.why: Not only A but also B는 A와 B를 모두 말해요.

items.q:
____ Some of them hunt at dawn, while others sleep all day and hunt at night. A few species even gather in groups to catch fish together.

Which sentence is the best opening for the paragraph?
o: Every bird hunts only at dawn.
Fish are the favorite food of all animals.
Birds use a surprising variety of hunting methods.
Sleeping all day is common among people who work at night.
items.why: 뒷 문장들을 모두 아우르는 주제문은 사냥 방식의 다양성이에요.

items.q:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Cats and dogs both make good pets. The former need less attention, while the latter need daily walks.

What does 'the latter' refer to?
o: cats
dogs
pets
walks
items.why: the latter는 나중에 언급된 대상인 dogs를 가리켜요.

items.q:
Which expression best completes the sentence?

The factory closed last spring; ____, hundreds of workers lost their jobs.
o: as a result
on the other hand
for example
in contrast
items.why: 공장 폐쇄의 결과를 나타내므로 as a result가 알맞아요.

items.q:
When you summarize, you can replace a list with one general word.

Which word can replace 'apples, pears and cherries'?
o: vegetables
flowers
juice
fruit
items.why: 사과, 배, 체리를 묶는 상위어는 fruit예요.

items.q:
The study found that students who walked to school arrived more alert than those who came by car. The researchers recommend keeping walking routes short and safe.

Which sentence does NOT belong in an accurate summary because it adds the summarizer's own opinion?
o: Students who walked to school arrived more alert than others.
Researchers recommend short, safe walking routes.
Walking to school is obviously the best habit anyone can have.
The study compared two common ways of getting to school each day.
items.why: 'obviously the best habit'은 글에 없는 요약자의 의견이에요.

items.q:
Which sentence is the most concise and accurate summary of the one below?

Despite the fact that the weather was extremely cold, a large number of people decided to attend the outdoor event.
o: The cold weather stopped people from attending the outdoor event.
Many people attended the outdoor event despite the cold.
Very few people came to the outdoor event because it was cold.
The outdoor event was cancelled because of the extreme cold.
items.why: 추위에도 불구하고 많은 사람이 참석했다는 의미를 간결하게 담은 문장이에요.

items.q:
Which phrase best completes the paragraph?

Many people think that more homework improves grades. ____, several studies suggest the opposite.
o: On the other hand
As a result
In the same way
For the same reason
items.why: 일반적 믿음과 반대되는 내용을 시작하므로 On the other hand가 알맞아요.

items.q:
What is the relationship between the two parts of the sentence below?

Critics argue that the plan is too costly, whereas supporters claim it will save money.
o: cause and effect
time order
example
contrast
